This work establishes a direct comparison between video and tracking modalities for group activity recognition (GAR) in team sports. The core innovation lies in the role-aware positional graph (RPG) architecture, which encodes player positions and roles into a structured graph representation. Each node represents an entity (player or ball) with 8-dimensional features including position, velocity, and role. Edges are constructed based on tactical line adjacency, enabling the model to capture spatial and role-based interactions. The tracking backbone uses a DeepGCN with GIN layers to process these graphs, followed by temporal pooling and a classifier. This architecture outperforms video models by 16.9 points in balanced accuracy while using 479× fewer parameters. The video backbone leverages Vision Transformers (VideoMAE) for frame-level encoding. The study's key insight is that tracking data, when properly structured, can match or exceed video performance with significantly lower computational cost. The findings suggest that for GSE’s NGS-replacement lane, tracking-based models are superior due to their efficiency and robustness to data scarcity. However, the absence of multimodal fusion and reliance on high-quality tracking data limit generalizability.
